earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog: only Collins comparative wordlist data (1977-2003) showing Piru is a dialect of Luhu; no phonological description found.

new_statements.quote: [p.82] An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe. Note too Asilulu palaʔekni [paláʔekən] 'recall him' and Luhu palaʔeʔena [palaʔeʔéna]. ... This obligatory penultimate stress rule ... seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable. [p.79] If one compares Luhu and Piru, one notices no significant sound differences.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Ch. V sec. 4 'Luhu and Hoamoal', p.82 (PDF p.92); identity statement p.79 (PDF p.89); cf. pp.82-83 and fn.116-117 (p.145)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (symlink to, ANU Pacific Linguistics D-47 open-access scan, 178 pp., text layer present) plus the saved 150-dpi render and the extracted text extract. At printed p.82 (PDF p.92) the page image reads exactly: 'An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu(116) húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe. Note too…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Luhu (of which Piru is a dialect) and the other Hoamoal languages, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word, counting suffixes and enclitic particles/petrified postposed demonstratives (e.g. hulán-e 'moon', palaʔeʔé-na), so stress moves rightward whenever material is added; this contrasts with Asilulu, where stress stays on the root penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Luhu; Collins notes the rule interacts with the many obligatory suffixes/postparticles in Hoamoal languages (fn.117: Luhu -e is permanently suffixed to nouns ending in non-high vowels or n/t) and that it drives antepenultimate vowel deletion in a few items (kallana 'wave', sumbeke 'shove', mandae 'male').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress including suffixes and cliticised particles (stress domain = phonological word with enclitics); based on Collins's own 1977-79 fieldnotes on Luhu and Piru; examples are citation forms. Statement is made for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole and exemplified with Luhu; Piru is covered via Collins's explicit claim (p.79) that Piru and Luhu show no significant sound differences.
new_statements.identity_note: piru1241 'Piru' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 [ppr] was merged with [lcq] Luhu (CR 2011-084, 2012-096; final name Luhu, code lcq), and Glottolog's language-level entry is luhu1243 'Luhu-Piru'. Collins 1983 (pp.79-81), from his own 1977-79 fieldwork, treats Piru (a handful of speakers over sixty at Piru village, head of Piru Bay) as a dialect of Luhu with 'no significant sound differences', differing mainly in loss of verbal conjugations and Eti/Alune loanwords. The quoted stress rule is stated for the Hoamoal branch of West Piru Bay (Luhu, Manipa, Boano, Kelang, Wakasihu) and exemplified with Luhu forms; no Piru form is cited with stress marked. Any catalog entry should be filed under luhu1243 (Luhu, Hoamoal peninsula, west Seram) with Piru as a covered dialect, not as an independent language.
